summary: RESULT: the best PPO model reached the target in the high-fidelity N-body check: a = 2.6831 AU, e = 0.0070 after 7,000 simulated years, and the orbit stayed within tolerance for 200 ballistic years with the Moon bound.

Direction: the impulse-weighted recoil direction on Earth has along-track (prograde) cosine 0.99, |radial| 0.10, |out-of-plane| 0.07; 0.0% of the impulse was retrograde. Along-track thrust raises orbital energy fastest (Gauss: da/dt = 2 a^2 v f_T / mu, with f_T the along-track acceleration); radial/normal components mostly waste reaction mass.

Launch speed: mass-weighted mean 2.493e+06 m/s vs 2.355e+06 m/s, the minimum-energy speed that uses the whole asteroid (heuristic uses 2.480e+06 m/s). Momentum per joule falls as 2/u, so a lower speed saves energy but costs more mass.

Most effective decisions (largest da per 100-y interval, fast model): t=7000 y: da=+0.0546 AU (prograde cos 0.99, u=2.60e+06 m/s, throttle 0.56); t=6900 y: da=+0.0514 AU (prograde cos 0.98, u=2.58e+06 m/s, throttle 0.55); t=6100 y: da=+0.0421 AU (prograde cos 0.98, u=2.61e+06 m/s, throttle 0.54). Least effective: t=100 y: da=+0.0098 AU (prograde cos 1.00, u=2.40e+06 m/s, throttle 0.46). At similar throttle, gains per interval grow with a, because at constant thrust acceleration da/dt ~ a^1.5.
Timing: ejected in 70 of 70 decision intervals (first 100 y, last 7000 y). It keeps thrusting until the orbit enters the target window, where the episode ends.
Resources (high-fidelity run): PPO used 94.9% of the asteroid and 59.4% of the energy budget; heuristic 95.2% / 58.5%; no-ejection baseline stays at a = 1.0000 AU.
Versus the hand-designed heuristic: PPO arrives slower (7,000 vs 3,600 y) and uses more energy.
This is the best model found in the tested training run, not a proven global optimum.

feasibility.verdict: FEASIBLE within this model (physically hypothetical scale)
lines: Required slow-spiral delta-v 1 -> 2.7 AU: 11,658 m/s (Hohmann two-impulse: 10,997 m/s)
Orbital energy change of Earth+Moon: 1.697e+33 J; angular momentum change 1.741e+40 kg m^2/s
Average power just for the orbital energy change over 10,000 y: 5.377e+21 W  (= 3.10e+04 x all sunlight intercepted by Earth)
Minimum launch energy with this reservoir: 1.664e+35 J -> average power 5.273e+23 W (= 1.38e-03 x total solar luminosity)
Reaction mass needed at max speed: 1.415e+22 kg (0.193 lunar masses); available 3.000e+22 kg
Max launch speed = 1.67% of c (non-relativistic model; error grows above ~10% c)

Solar collectors: 30% of the Sun's output = 1.148e+26 W intercepted at 0.5 AU; electricity delivered to the arms 1.290e+25 W with Earth at 1 AU, 1.114e+25 W at 2.7 AU; launcher peak demand (max packet rate and speed) 6.338e+24 W -> the beams supply 1.76x the peak demand
[OK ] mass: needs launch speed 2.355e+06 m/s with ALL 3.00e+22 kg; max allowed 5.000e+06 m/s (mass-limited delta-v capacity 2.475e+04 m/s vs required 1.166e+04 m/s)
[OK ] energy: minimum energy drawn 1.664e+35 J vs available 3.817e+36 J (reserve 3.000e+35 J + collectors 1.114e+25 W x 10,000 y)
[OK ] rate: at max packet rate and speed the transfer needs >= 1,771 years (mission 10,000 y)
[OK ] combined: slowest speed meeting mass AND time limits 2.355e+06 m/s -> needs 3.000e+22 kg and 1.664e+35 J
plain: To move Earth from 1 AU to 2.7 AU slowly, its orbital speed must be changed by about 11.7 km/s in total (it ends up slower, but on a much bigger orbit).
Mass: OK - throwing the whole asteroid at 2,355 km/s gives enough push.
Energy: OK - the cheapest way needs 1.66e+35 J; the solar collectors deliver 1.11e+25 W (1.8x the launcher's peak demand), i.e. up to 3.82e+36 J over the mission, plus a reserve of 3.00e+35 J.
Time: OK - at full thrust the transfer takes at least 1,771 years; the mission allows 10,000.
This is an analytic estimate for a slow spiral; the simulation then shows what actually happens.

disclaimer: This is the best policy found in this training run, judged on a few deterministic test episodes. It is not proven to be globally optimal; other strategies (e.g. the heuristic) can be better on some measures.
Reward is only the scoring rule used to train the agent. Mission success is judged separately from physics: final a, e and inclination, a ballistic stability check, and the Moon staying bound.
